snippet.description: There is a statistic that tends to stop people cold when they first hear it. During the golden age of piracy, which ran roughly from the 1650s through to the 1730s, disease killed somewhere between five and ten sailors for every one who died in battle. Not wounded, not captured, not lost at sea in a storm, but killed outright by illness on ships that were otherwise sailing fine, crewed by men who had survived everything the ocean threw at them. And if you trace a significant share of those deaths back to their source, you end up in the same place every time: the question of where two hundred men on a wooden ship actually went to the toilet.
